bp: Fact-checks do more than state that a claim is false. They also try to move a reader from belief, doubt, or confusion toward acceptance of the correction. That means the wording itself matters: a debunk can cite evidence calmly, appeal to credibility, use loaded phrasing, point to danger, mock the false claim, or invite the reader to judge for themselves. This paper studies that layer of fact-checking by comparing community-written debunks from Community Notes with professionally written debunks from EUvsDisinfo and the Database of Known Fakes. The real-world question is whether crowd fact-checking changes the style of correction. A common worry is that volunteer notes might rely more on subjective or persuasive language than institutional fact-checkers. The study asks a more careful question: how many persuasion techniques appear, what kinds appear, and how the crowd rates notes that use them.
wh: The hard part is that persuasion is not the same as lying, and it is not automatically bad. A fact-check can be accurate and still use language that pushes the reader emotionally. Some persuasive moves may help a correction feel clear and useful; others may make it sound biased, condescending, or manipulative. The comparison is also uneven because Community Notes, EUvsDisinfo, and DBKF are different ecosystems. They have different authors, institutional rules, audiences, topics, and rating processes. If one source uses more of a certain rhetorical technique, that difference may reflect who writes the debunk, what topics they cover, or what norms the platform rewards. The paper therefore cannot just count strong adjectives and declare one ecosystem more subjective. It must separate average prevalence, type of technique, systematic differences, and crowd reactions to particular problematic rhetorical means.
naive: A smart beginner might read a sample of community notes and professional debunks, mark the ones that sound opinionated, and compare the totals. That fails for three reasons. First, persuasion has many forms, so a single impression of subjectivity hides whether the text appeals to emotion, authority, urgency, ridicule, or other devices. Second, small samples can be dominated by topic mix: war propaganda, health rumors, and platform rumors may naturally invite different wording. Third, the key question is not only whether persuasion appears, but how readers evaluate it. A note with extra persuasive elements may be seen as helpful overall while still being penalized when it uses a specific troubling tactic.
ap: The paper's central move is to treat debunks as comparable pieces of corrective writing and to measure rhetorical technique across large collections rather than relying on anecdotes about crowd quality. It gathers debunks from Community Notes, EUvsDisinfo, and DBKF, then quantifies both the amount and the type of persuasive language used in each ecosystem. This lets the study test the prior hypothesis directly: do community-produced debunks contain more persuasion techniques on average than professional fact-checks? The answer reported in the abstract is no. The deeper result is not that all debunks sound the same. The study finds systematic rhetorical differences, which it ties to institutional norms and topic coverage. It then uses Community Notes rating data to ask how the crowd responds: more persuasive elements are associated with slightly higher helpfulness, but raters still penalize particular problematic rhetorical means.
mech: The mechanism begins with three sources of debunking text. Community Notes supplies crowd-authored corrections that are also judged by crowd raters. EUvsDisinfo and DBKF supply professional or institutionally curated debunks. Each debunk is treated as a document whose wording can contain recognizable persuasion techniques. The study then maps text into counts and categories: how many persuasive elements appear, and which types appear. Those measurements allow several comparisons. First, it compares average prevalence across community and professional ecosystems, which tests the claim that Community Notes are more persuasion-heavy overall. Second, it compares the mix of rhetorical techniques, because two systems may have the same average number while using different styles. Third, it connects those differences to the source setting: professional debunking bodies have institutional norms and recurring topical domains, while Community Notes has a crowd process and the topics that users bring to the platform. Finally, for Community Notes, the paper links rhetorical measurements to crowd helpfulness judgments. The output is not a new fact-checking classifier. It is an empirical picture: overall counts, technique-level differences, and evidence about which kinds of persuasive wording the crowd rewards or punishes.
math: The main mathematical idea is measurement by coding text into comparable signals. A debunk is ordinary language, but comparison requires turning parts of that language into counted objects: this sentence contains a certain rhetorical move; that debunk contains several; this ecosystem has a different mix from another. Counting is simple only after the hard definition work is done, because the unit being counted must mean the same thing across sources. The next idea is comparison between groups. The paper asks whether the average number of persuasion techniques differs between crowd and professional debunks. An average is a compression: it turns many documents into one typical value, which is useful for testing a broad hypothesis but can hide differences in which techniques appear. That is why technique types matter alongside totals. The Community Notes part adds association between wording and ratings. A helpfulness rating is a crowd judgment, and the study examines whether it rises or falls with measured persuasive elements. This is not proof that wording causes the rating, because topics and note quality may also matter. It is evidence about how measured rhetoric and crowd evaluation move together.
dots: This paper sits inside the conference's broader misinformation and trust family, where the shared problem is that trust cannot be reduced to a true-or-false label. Neighboring papers in the same batch study document-level claim extraction aligned with expert values and online discourse analysis across claims, arguments, and opinions. This paper handles the next step in that chain: after a claim is identified and checked, how is the correction worded, and how do people judge that wording? It also connects to recurring ideas about ranking and evaluation, because Community Notes depends on crowd helpfulness ratings to decide which corrections surface. Unlike papers that retrieve evidence, detect fake videos, or calibrate model confidence, this one studies the social presentation of truth. Its contribution is to show that debunking quality includes rhetoric, institutional norms, topic coverage, and crowd judgment, not just factual accuracy.
ww: The approach works better than the naive story because it tests the common suspicion at the right level of detail. If someone only asks whether Community Notes feel more subjective, they may mistake a few vivid examples for a general pattern. Large-scale counting reduces that risk by forcing the comparison across many debunks. If someone only compares one total count, they may miss the more interesting fact that ecosystems can differ in rhetorical style without differing in average amount. Looking at technique types catches that structure. The Community Notes rating analysis adds another layer: it recognizes that the crowd is not merely producing text but also judging text. The reported finding is subtle. Notes with more persuasive elements receive slightly higher helpfulness ratings overall, so persuasion is not simply rejected. Yet raters penalize particular problematic rhetorical means, which suggests they distinguish useful forceful explanation from wording they see as inappropriate. That distinction is exactly what a first-principles account of debunking needs.
po: The payoff is a clearer account of what community fact-checking is and is not doing rhetorically. The paper reports no evidence that Community Notes contain a higher average number of persuasion techniques than professional fact-checks, which challenges a simple criticism of crowd-authored debunks. At the same time, it identifies systematic differences in rhetorical style across ecosystems, so the result is not a claim that all fact-checking institutions write alike. For platform designers and misinformation researchers, the useful capability is diagnostic: they can inspect which persuasive devices appear, where they appear, and how crowd raters respond to them.
limits: The abstract supports a large-scale comparison, but it does not prove that persuasion techniques cause higher helpfulness ratings. More persuasive notes may also be clearer, more detailed, or attached to topics where readers already agree. The comparison depends on how persuasion techniques are defined and detected; if the coding misses subtle rhetoric or treats unlike phrases as the same move, the counts can mislead. The sources also differ in institutional role and topical coverage, so not every difference should be read as an author-quality difference. The findings are grounded in Community Notes, EUvsDisinfo, and DBKF, and may not transfer unchanged to other languages, platforms, crises, or moderation rules.
